problemText: A weather reporter on the evening news says: 'Right now, the temperature is 12 degrees Celsius and it is raining.' Is this a weather statement or a climate statement, and why?
choices: It is a climate statement because the reporter is giving information about rain and temperature.
It is a weather statement because it describes the atmosphere at a specific moment in time, not an average across many years.
It is a climate statement because rain and temperature collected over time establish what a region's typical conditions are.
It is a weather statement because the words 'right now' indicate a single point in time rather than a long-term pattern.
hints: Ask yourself: does this describe what is happening RIGHT NOW at one moment, or does it describe a pattern built from many years of records?
Look for timescale clues in the sentence — words like 'right now' or 'average' or 'typical' tell you whether you are looking at weather or climate.

problemText: A student writes: 'Yesterday it was 28 degrees Celsius and sunny in my town, so my town's climate must be warm and dry.' Explain what is wrong with this reasoning.
choices: The student is confusing climate with latitude, which determines whether a place is warm or cold.
The student is correct — a warm, sunny day is the best evidence of a warm, dry climate in any region.
The student is confusing one day of weather with a long-term climate pattern; climate requires many years of averaged records, not a single day.
The student should have said 'yesterday's weather' instead of 'my town's climate,' but the conclusion about the climate is still correct.
hints: Climate is defined by averaging records over how many years — one day, one week, or many decades?
Could a region have a cold, wet climate overall but still have one warm, sunny day? Think about whether that one day would prove the climate is warm and dry.

problemText: A town's official climate records, collected over 35 years, show that summer temperatures average 26 degrees Celsius. On one summer day this year, the temperature reaches 38 degrees Celsius. Which description is correct?
choices: The 38-degree day changes the town's climate record because one hot day proves the climate is getting hotter over the full period.
The 38-degree day means the town's climate record will now show an average of 32 degrees Celsius instead of 26 degrees Celsius when recalculated.
The 38-degree day raises the overall average slightly because adding one new temperature reading of 38 degrees will shift the total sum used in calculating the mean.
The 38-degree day is unusual weather for that town, but by itself it does not change the long-term climate average that was built from 35 years of data.
hints: Does one reading on one day change an average that was built from thousands of daily readings across 35 years?
Climate is the average; weather is the actual conditions on any one day. Can an unusual weather event replace a multi-decade average all by itself?

problemText: Three pieces of information are given about Location F: (1) 'Today, the wind is gusting up to 40 kilometers per hour.' (2) 'Over the last 30 years, Location F's average wind speed has been 15 kilometers per hour.' (3) 'Last week, Location F had three days of rain in a row.' Which statement or statements describe Location F's climate, and why do the others not?
choices: Only statement 2 describes climate because it is based on 30 years of averaged records; statements 1 and 3 describe specific short-term conditions, not an average.
Statements 1 and 3 both describe climate because they document actual wind speeds and precipitation events that represent the typical weather patterns at that location.
Only statement 1 describes climate because it measures wind speed in kilometers per hour, which is the standard unit that climate scientists use to quantify atmospheric conditions.
Statements 2 and 3 describe climate together because one provides the long-term average wind speed and one gives a specific rainfall event that illustrates how that average behaves in practice.
hints: Look at the timescale in each statement: which one names a long span with the word 'average,' and which ones name a specific day or short period?
Climate requires averaged records from many years to be properly defined. Does a single day's wind, or three consecutive days of rain, give you enough data to know the long-term average?

problemText: Location G has a climate described as 'dry, with very little rain.' One winter, Location G receives twice as much rain as it normally does in an entire year, spread across the season. A scientist checks Location G's 50-year climate records before and after that winter and finds the climate description remains unchanged at 'dry, with very little rain.' Explain why the unusually rainy winter did not change Location G's official climate description.
choices: The scientist made an error; a winter with twice the normal yearly rain should have changed the climate description because any increase in precipitation alters the official classification.
One season of above-average rain is weather, not climate. Climate is defined by a 50-year average of all years together, and one season cannot overpower 49 other years of records.
The climate description did not change because the extra rain was spread across the whole season rather than concentrated in one month, so it had less impact on the yearly total.
The winter did change the climate temporarily, but the long-term records automatically adjusted back to the original description after that season ended and new years were added to the average.
hints: What timescale defines climate — one season or many years averaged together?
If 49 years of dry data are already averaged into the 50-year record, how much weight does one season of extra rain have in that average?

problemText: A student makes four claims about two locations that both have 'cold, snowy climates' based on 40 years of averaged records: Claim A: 'Both locations will have snow on the ground every single day of winter.' Claim B: 'Both locations must have at least one day next winter when it is not snowing.' Claim C: 'A record-breaking warm day could occur in either location's upcoming winter and would disprove its climate classification.' Claim D: 'Both locations' official climate records would only change if their typical winter conditions shifted across many future years.' Which claim correctly reflects the relationship between weather and climate for these two locations?
choices: Claim A, because a snowy climate means it snows all the time without exception on every day of every winter.
Claim B, because a snowy climate does not guarantee continuous snow, only that snow is typical across many winters overall.
Claim D and also Claim B together, because climates can vary day to day but only change when the long-term average shifts, and a climate does not promise every single day matches the pattern.
Claim C, because a single warm day anywhere in the region's upcoming winter would prove that the snowy climate classification was incorrect from the start.
hints: A climate statement describes the typical pattern across many years; does it predict what must happen on every single day, or what usually happens overall?
If one unusual day of weather could overturn a 40-year climate average, how stable could any climate classification ever be?

problemText: What does latitude describe about a location on Earth? Which answer gives the correct definition?
choices: How close a location is to a large body of water.
How high a location sits above sea level.
How far north or south of the equator a location sits.
How much rain or snow a location receives each year.
hints: The lesson vocabulary section defines latitude as a measure of position relative to a specific line on Earth.
Think about the equator and the poles — what is being measured between them?

problemText: A mountain town and a nearby valley town sit at the same latitude and are both far from any ocean. The mountain town sits at 3,000 meters elevation, while the valley town sits at 200 meters elevation. Based on what you learned about elevation's effect on climate, which town would you expect to have cooler typical temperatures?
choices: The valley town, because it is closer to sea level where the sun's warmth is stronger.
The mountain town, because it is farther from the equator.
Both towns, because they share the same latitude and distance from water.
The mountain town, because higher elevation typically results in cooler typical temperatures.
hints: Both towns receive the same angle of sunlight and neither has water nearby to moderate temperature, so focus only on the one factor that differs.
The lesson states a clear rule about how elevation affects temperature — apply it directly.

problemText: Two coastal cities sit at low elevation right next to the same large ocean, but City X is located close to the equator while City Y is located much farther north, closer to a pole. Which statement correctly explains why their typical climates would differ?
choices: City X receives sunlight at a more direct angle throughout the year, making it typically warmer with smaller swings between seasons, while City Y receives slanting sunlight and is typically cooler with larger swings between seasons.

City X receives sunlight at a steep angle year-round due to its equatorial location, so it stays warm with little seasonal change, whereas City Y's higher latitude means sunlight hits at a shallow angle, producing cooler temperatures and dramatic seasonal temperature shifts.

City Y is positioned closer to a pole where the atmosphere is thinner, reducing the amount of solar radiation that can penetrate to the surface, which explains why it experiences colder typical temperatures compared to City X at the equator.

City X has a larger ocean surface area nearby that warms it constantly, while City Y's polar location means ocean water is frozen most of the year and cannot moderate temperature as effectively, making City Y much colder and more seasonal.
hints: Elevation and distance from water are the same for both cities, so the difference must come from latitude.
Remember that at the equator, sunlight arrives close to straight down, while near the poles it arrives at a low, slanting angle — how does this affect typical temperature and seasonal swings?

problemText: Region P sits at low elevation, close to the equator, and far inland, hundreds of kilometers from any ocean or large lake. Region Q sits at higher elevation, at the same latitude as Region P, and right next to a large ocean. Considering all three factors — latitude, elevation, and distance from water — which of the following correctly compares their typical climates?
choices: Region P would be warmer year-round with smaller seasonal swings and more precipitation because it is close to the equator and far from any ocean, so solar heating is strong and consistent without water to moderate temperature changes.

Region Q would be cooler because of its higher elevation, would have smaller seasonal swings because of the nearby ocean, and would likely receive more precipitation from the ocean, even though both regions share the same latitude.

Region Q would be cooler because of its higher elevation, but it would swing more between seasons because being at higher elevation amplifies seasonal extremes, and it would be drier because the elevation prevents moisture from rising.

Region P would have a hotter and more variable climate because it sits far from the ocean where temperature swings are extreme, while Region Q stays moderate because water moderates temperature, even though higher elevation in Region Q works against this moderation effect.
hints: Both regions share the same latitude, so that factor is equal — focus on how elevation and distance from water differ, and apply what the lesson teaches about each.
Consider how elevation affects temperature, how a large body of water moderates temperature swings, and how water is a source of nearby moisture.

problemText: A student is trying to predict the typical climate of a location that sits at the same latitude as another well-known location, but much farther from any ocean. The student says: 'Since they are at the same latitude, they must have the same typical temperature and precipitation pattern.' Is this reasoning correct, and why or why not?
choices: Yes, the reasoning is correct, because latitude is the only factor that determines how much heat a location receives from the sun and sets the climate pattern.
No, the reasoning is incorrect, because locations closer to the equator always receive more precipitation no matter how far they are from water sources like oceans or lakes.

No, the reasoning is incorrect. Although both locations receive the same angle of sunlight, elevation and distance from water are different and will create different typical temperature and precipitation patterns.

Yes, the reasoning is correct, because latitude determines the angle of sunlight and that angle is the main force that shapes climate, while elevation and distance from water are only minor influences.
hints: The lesson explicitly warns against assuming that shared latitude alone means similar climates — what else needs to be checked?
Review the worked example in the lesson where Region B and Region C sit at the same latitude but have very different climates because of different elevation and distance from water.

problemText: A travel guide describes two mountain regions that are both located far from any ocean, far from the equator, and therefore both tend to be cold. However, one mountain region (A) sits at 2,500 meters elevation while the other mountain region (B) sits at 1,200 meters elevation. A visitor asks: 'Will both regions have the same typical winter temperatures?' Based on the three factors from this lesson, explain which region would be expected to have colder typical winter temperatures and why, even though both share the same latitude and distance from water.
choices: Both regions will have equally cold winters because they are both far from the equator and far from water, so latitude and distance from water are the dominant factors that set winter temperature at any location.

Neither region's winter temperature can be predicted because elevation changes so dramatically across mountains that it overwhelms the effects of latitude and distance from water in ways that require local data to know.
Region B will have colder typical winter temperatures because it is at lower elevation and therefore sits closer to the troposphere where cold air masses from the poles can more easily reach it.

Region A will have colder typical winter temperatures because it sits at a higher elevation, and the lesson teaches that higher elevation typically means cooler typical temperatures, even when comparing two locations at the same latitude and far from water.
hints: Two of the three factors (latitude and distance from water) are the same, so focus on how the third factor — elevation — differs and apply what the lesson taught.
The lesson gives a real-world example of a mountain town and a valley town at the same latitude — which one is colder?

problemText: A surface current is described as a warm current. What does this mean?
choices: The current flows only during the warm months of the year.
The water in the current started near the equator and has not cooled down yet.
The water in the current is always warm enough to swim in comfortably.
The water in the current is warmer than the ocean water surrounding it at that location.
hints: Think about the definition: warm or cold is a comparison, not a fixed temperature number.
A current keeps its label based on how it compares to what is around it right now, not where it came from or the calendar.

problemText: The North Atlantic Current flows east toward the coast of northwestern Europe after bending away from the coast of the United States. This current carries warm water from near the Gulf of Mexico. Based on the current's starting point and direction, what should you predict about the winter climate of northwestern Europe?
choices: Winters should be milder than at other places at the same latitude, because warm water from the tropics flows alongside the coast.
Winters should be much colder than at other places at the same latitude, because the current flows so far north.
Winters should be about the same as other places at the same latitude, because climate depends only on how far north a place is.
Winters should be warmer than places near the Gulf of Mexico, because the current moves toward colder water.
hints: Trace the current's starting point—where is it warm?—and follow it forward to where it reaches the coastline.
The lesson says the offshore water next to a coastline becomes part of that coastline's climate. What kind of water is next to northwestern Europe?

problemText: Two students are looking at a map of ocean currents near the east coast of Canada. One current flows south from Arctic waters, and another flows north from warmer mid-Atlantic waters. The first student says, 'Both currents flow in opposite directions, so they will have opposite effects on the coast.' Is this reasoning correct? Why or why not?
choices: Yes, because any current flowing south has a cooling effect and any current flowing north has a warming effect.
No, because a current's effect depends on whether its water is warmer or colder than the water around it, not just on which compass direction it flows.
Yes, because the Labrador Current and Gulf Stream are named opposites and do the opposite things.
No, because currents that flow north always stay warm and currents that flow south always stay cold, so the direction alone tells you the effect.
hints: What makes a current 'warm' or 'cold' according to the lesson? Is it the direction it flows, or something else?
A current starting in the tropics and flowing north stays warm because it stays warmer than what surrounds it. What about a current starting in the Arctic and flowing south?

problemText: A student is comparing two coastal towns, San Diego and Charleston, that sit at nearly the same latitude along the United States coast. The student notices that San Diego's winter temperatures are milder than Charleston's. The student first thinks, 'They must be at different latitudes,' but then checks a map and finds they are almost the same distance from the equator. What information from the lesson would help the student explain why the climates are actually different despite similar latitudes?
choices: San Diego must be at a higher elevation than Charleston, which means the air temperature drops with altitude and makes San Diego's winters consistently colder regardless of any ocean effects.
Charleston must be on a peninsula that extends farther into the ocean, which exposes it to stronger winds that cool the air during winter months more than San Diego experiences.
San Diego must have a different ocean current running along its coast than Charleston does, which pushes its winter climate milder or cooler than latitude alone would predict.
San Diego must receive more rain from its ocean current, which increases cloud cover and thereby traps heat in the atmosphere to keep winters warmer year-round.
hints: The lesson says a current's effect stacks on top of latitude and other factors. If two places are at the same latitude but different climates, what could the difference be?
Trace what kind of current runs along each coast. Does one carry warmer water than the other?

problemText: A cold current starts near the Arctic and flows south along a coastline toward lower latitudes. As it flows south, the surrounding ocean water becomes warmer. Using the definition of a cold current, explain whether this current remains a cold current throughout its journey south, or whether it should be reclassified at some point.
choices: It stops being a cold current once it reaches the latitude where the surrounding water is warm, because the current itself will have warmed up by then and can no longer be classified as cold.
It is no longer either a warm or cold current once it crosses the equator, because the rotation of Earth changes the direction and properties of all water currents in the southern hemisphere.
It becomes a warm current by the time it reaches lower latitudes, because the current will have absorbed enough heat from the surrounding water to match tropical ocean temperatures.
It remains a cold current for as long as it is colder than the ocean water it is flowing through, even if the surrounding water is warmer at lower latitudes than it was near the Arctic.
hints: Warm and cold are comparisons: a current's label depends on whether it is warmer or colder than what surrounds it right then, not on a fixed temperature.
Does the Labrador Current stay a cold current the entire way south even though it flows toward warmer water? Use that example to think through this one.

problemText: Two explorers sail along different coasts at the 50° north latitude. Explorer A travels past the coast of northwestern Europe, where the warm North Atlantic Current flows. Explorer B travels past the coast of eastern Canada, where the cold Labrador Current flows. Both explorers measure the winter air temperature and compare it to what their maps predict the climate should be at 50° north latitude (based only on how far north the location is). Which explorer would most likely measure an air temperature warmer than the map predicts, and which would measure a temperature colder than the map predicts? Use the concept of how a current's origin and direction determine its effect.
choices: Explorer A would measure warmer than predicted, because the North Atlantic Current starts in the tropics and carries warm water that keeps the nearby air milder than latitude alone would suggest. Explorer B would measure colder than predicted, because the Labrador Current starts near the Arctic and carries cold water that keeps the nearby air cooler than latitude alone would suggest.

Explorer B would measure warmer than predicted, because the Labrador Current originates in tropical regions and transports heat energy northward along the coast, raising air temperatures above the latitude baseline. Explorer A would measure colder than predicted, because the North Atlantic Current loses thermal energy as it travels northward and becomes dominated by colder Arctic water masses.

Both explorers would measure temperatures significantly warmer than predicted, because ocean currents always transport heat from the equator and enhance warming at higher latitudes regardless of whether they originate in warm or cold regions, making latitude irrelevant to climate prediction.

Explorer A would measure colder than predicted, because currents lose their heat energy as they travel long distances northward and dissipate into surrounding water. Explorer B would measure warmer than predicted, because the Labrador Current flows southward and accumulates thermal energy from equatorial regions before reaching 50° north.
hints: Trace each current from its origin to its effect: where does it start, what temperature water does it carry, and what does that do to the coastline's climate?

The worked examples show that the United Kingdom (with the warm Gulf Stream) has mild winters, and Newfoundland (with the Labrador Current) has cold ones, even though they are at similar latitudes. Use that pattern here.

problemText: A climatograph shows twelve monthly average temperatures and twelve monthly average precipitations for one location. What does the annual temperature range tell you about that location?
choices: The difference between the warmest month's average temperature and the coldest month's average temperature
How much the temperature changes each day based on the overnight low and daytime high throughout the year
The total amount of heat energy measured in calories that the location receives from the sun annually
Whether the location experiences more rainfall or snowfall depending on its distance from the equator
hints: Think about what 'annual' means and what 'range' means when talking about two different months.
The annual temperature range is a math calculation using two specific numbers from the climatograph.

problemText: A location's monthly average temperatures in degrees Celsius from January through December are: 15, 16, 18, 21, 25, 28, 30, 29, 26, 22, 18, 15. Calculate the annual temperature range for this location.
choices: 12 degrees Celsius
15 degrees Celsius
18 degrees Celsius
30 degrees Celsius
hints: You need to find which month is warmest and which month is coldest, then subtract.
The warmest month shown here is 30 degrees Celsius; find the coldest month and do the subtraction.

problemText: Location X has monthly precipitation in millimeters of: 120, 115, 98, 45, 12, 5, 3, 4, 8, 35, 95, 110. Which statement correctly describes the wet and dry seasons at Location X?
choices: Location X has no wet season because no month receives more than 120 millimeters
Location X is wet all year because every month receives at least 3 millimeters of rain
Location X has a wet season from December through March and a dry season from June through August
Location X has a dry season in May because that month receives less than the annual average
hints: Scan all twelve numbers and look for a stretch of months that are clearly higher than the others, and another stretch that is clearly lower.
The three highest numbers cluster around the beginning and end of the year, and the three lowest numbers are bunched in the middle months.

problemText: Location G's monthly average temperatures in degrees Celsius are: 12, 13, 15, 18, 22, 26, 28, 27, 24, 19, 15, 12. Location H's monthly average temperatures in degrees Celsius are: 24, 25, 23, 20, 16, 12, 10, 12, 15, 19, 22, 24. Both locations have an annual temperature range of about 16 degrees Celsius, yet they are in different hemispheres. Which pair of statements correctly explains why and identifies each location's hemisphere?
choices: Both locations have the same size range, so they must be in the same hemisphere because annual temperature range is the only factor that determines hemisphere location

Location H has its warmest months spread across the Northern Hemisphere summer season while Location G shows warming across the Southern Hemisphere summer season based on the calendar timing of peak temperatures
Location G receives more precipitation than Location H, which shows it is in the wetter Northern Hemisphere with stronger monsoon patterns

Location G's warmest months are June-August and coolest are December-February (Northern Hemisphere), while Location H's warmest months are December-February and coolest are June-August (Southern Hemisphere)
hints: Hemisphere is determined by which calendar months are warm and which are cool, not by the size of the temperature range.
Compare the position of the warmest and coldest numbers in each list to the calendar months January through December.

problemText: Location J's monthly precipitation totals (in millimeters) are: 85, 80, 70, 50, 25, 8, 4, 5, 15, 40, 65, 80. When you add all twelve numbers, the annual total is 527 millimeters. If three months account for 235 millimeters of that total, what does this reveal about Location J's climate pattern that a single wet month's number alone would not show?
choices: That more than 44 percent of Location J's yearly precipitation falls into just three months, revealing a strongly marked wet season rather than evenly distributed rain throughout the year

That Location J receives enough total precipitation each year to support ecosystems because 235 millimeters divided by twelve months gives an average monthly precipitation that plants can use for growth

That Location J's annual precipitation of 527 millimeters places it in a climate category between arid regions receiving under 250 millimeters annually and tropical zones receiving over 2000 millimeters annually

That Location J's range from 4 millimeters to 85 millimeters across its twelve months indicates seasonal variation, which proves the location experiences distinct periods of higher and lower water availability
hints: Calculate what fraction of the year's 527 millimeters those three months represent: 235 ÷ 527 ≈ 0.446 or about 44 percent.
The lesson teaches that adding all twelve numbers and comparing the total to parts of it shows whether precipitation is concentrated in a real season or spread evenly.

problemText: A student reads a climatograph for Location K and notices that January's average temperature is 22°C and January's precipitation is 180 millimeters. The student concludes: 'Location K must have a very wet climate because January alone shows a lot of rain.' Explain why this conclusion violates the one-month trap and what the student should do instead to read Location K's climate correctly. Which statement best identifies both the error and the correct method?
choices: The error is that 180 millimeters in one month cannot support the idea of a wet climate unless that same amount appears in every other month; the student should multiply January's precipitation by twelve to estimate whether the annual total would actually be considered wet

The error is that one month, even a wet one, does not prove the whole year's pattern without comparing all twelve months to each other and computing the annual total; the student should read all twelve precipitation numbers and check whether January is part of a longer wet season or an outlier

The error is that the student focused on precipitation while ignoring temperature, which is equally important for defining climate; the student should add January's temperature value to the precipitation value to create a combined climate index for Location K

The error is that without knowing Location K's latitude and longitude, a single month's data cannot establish climate patterns; the student should identify the geographic region first and then verify January's data matches known climate zones for that region
hints: The lesson teaches that comparing one month to the other eleven months is exactly what makes climate reading different from just reading one number off an axis.
Recall the worked example where 90 millimeters in January seemed large until compared to the annual total and the pattern of other months.
